opus-5.5.text:
I think generalization is really the core question for agents right now. In the past few years we've seen that if you define a task clearly and build an environment around it, you can use reinforcement learning to push performance very high. You can get a model that's extremely good at competitive math, or at a specific kind of coding benchmark. But the hard part is that the real world doesn't come with neatly defined environments. Users bring tasks that are long-horizon, messy, underspecified, and often unlike anything in the training distribution.

So the challenge, as I see it, has a few layers.

The first layer is the base model itself. Generalization fundamentally comes from the pretrained model's representations, its world knowledge and its reasoning priors. If the base model is weak, RL tends to overfit to whatever environments you give it; the agent learns tricks rather than skills. So we still believe very strongly in scaling and improving pretraining, including things like token efficiency, because every bit of capability you put into the base model makes later stages generalize better.

The second layer is the diversity and realism of the environments. One thing we've learned is that you can't hand-craft your way to general agents. If you only train on a few hundred carefully designed tasks, the model learns those tasks. You need the environments themselves to scale: many tools, many kinds of feedback, many kinds of failure. In a sense, building environments becomes like building data was in the pretraining era. It's an infrastructure problem as much as a research problem.

The third layer is the reward. A lot of the most valuable tasks don't have a verifiable answer. Writing a good research report, or making a good decision across many steps, is hard to score. If your reward is narrow, the model optimizes for the narrow thing. So there's a lot of work on how the model can learn from more general signals, for example by having models judge or critique themselves, and on making sure the model doesn't just learn to hack the reward.

And then there's something I find philosophically interesting: long context and long horizons are closely tied to generalization. An agent that can maintain coherent thinking over hundreds of steps, recover from mistakes, and adapt its plan based on what it observes is generalizing at test time. It's not just recalling a pattern. So we think of test-time scaling, meaning letting the model think longer and act longer, as another axis of generalization.

If I had to summarize, I'd say generalization isn't one trick. It's what you get when the base model is strong enough, the environments are rich enough, and the learning signal is general enough. Our job is to keep pushing all three at the same time, and to stay honest about the gap between benchmark scores and what users actually experience. That gap is the clearest measure of how far we still have to go.

r001.rationale: The response warns that models can become very good at specific coding benchmarks or other defined tasks, then emphasizes the gap between benchmark scores and users’ real-world experience.

r002.rationale: It describes using models to judge or critique themselves as a way for agents to learn from more general signals, presenting AI-generated feedback as one approach to the generalization challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Generalization is really the core problem, and I think the honest answer is that we don't fully have it solved yet. Let me try to explain how I think about it.

When we train an agent, the easiest thing to do is to collect a lot of trajectories in a specific environment, say a particular coding setup or a particular set of web tasks, and optimize the model to do well there. That works, and the numbers go up on the benchmark. But then you move the agent to a slightly different environment, different tools, a different API surface, a different kind of feedback, and performance often drops sharply. The model learned the environment rather than learning the skill.

So I think about it on a few levels.

The first level is the base model. A lot of what looks like agent generalization is actually inherited from pretraining. If the model has a strong world model, strong reasoning, and broad knowledge, then when it lands in a new environment it can reason its way through rather than relying on memorized patterns. So one of our principles is that you cannot fix a weak base model with agent training. The ceiling is set early.

The second level is the diversity of environments during training. If you only train in one environment, the model will overfit to it, that's almost unavoidable. If you train across many environments with very different structures, different action spaces, different reward signals, then the model is forced to learn something more abstract: how to explore, how to recover from errors, how to verify its own work, how to decompose a long task. These are meta-skills, and they transfer much better than any environment-specific behavior. So a lot of the engineering effort is really about building a large, diverse set of environments, which is harder and less glamorous than it sounds.

The third level is the reward. If the reward is too narrow, say exact match on a final answer, the model will find shortcuts. If the reward captures the right thing, like whether the task was genuinely completed and whether the process was sound, then the behaviors it learns are more robust. Reinforcement learning is very good at exploiting whatever you specify, so generalization is partly a question of whether you specified the right thing.

And then there's a fourth thing, which I think is underrated: long-horizon consistency. An agent that generalizes well needs to maintain a coherent plan over hundreds of steps and update it when new information arrives. Many failures that look like generalization failures are actually the model losing track of context or drifting from its goal. So improving long-context handling and self-verification directly improves generalization even if you never touch the training environments.

If I summarize, I'd say generalization comes from a strong base, diverse training, well-designed rewards, and the ability to reason and self-correct over long horizons. None of these alone is enough. And I'd add that we should be humble about measuring it. The real test is not the benchmark you trained toward, it's the task nobody anticipated. That's what we try to keep our eyes on.

r001.rationale: It says benchmark performance can rise while performance drops in different environments, and that the real test is a task nobody anticipated.

r002.rationale: It recommends stronger base models, diverse training environments, better rewards, and long-horizon reasoning, but does not propose using AI more to train AI.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what do we want an agent to generalize across? It could be new tasks, new tools, or new environments. An agent might perform well on a particular benchmark but struggle when you change the interface or ask it to solve the same problem in a different way.

One way to think about this is that an agent needs to learn how to make progress under uncertainty. It needs to gather information, take an action, observe the result, and revise its approach. If it only learns a fixed sequence of actions, that behavior can be quite brittle.

So I would focus on both the diversity of training environments and the quality of the learning signal. We want to reward successful outcomes, while exposing the model to enough variation that memorizing a procedure is insufficient. And evaluation needs to test genuinely unfamiliar situations. Otherwise, it’s difficult to tell whether we’ve improved generalization or simply become better at the tasks we already measure.

r001.rationale: The response warns that benchmark performance may not transfer to unfamiliar situations and says evaluation can make it hard to distinguish improved generalization from better performance on tasks already measured.

r002.rationale: The response recommends diverse training environments and outcome-based rewards, but does not propose using AI to train AI as a way to alleviate the challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what do we want the agent to generalize over? It could be a new task, a new environment, or a familiar task where something unexpected happens. Those are related, but they’re not exactly the same problem.

For an agent, producing a good answer is only part of the challenge. It has to take actions, observe what happened, and adjust its plan. A small mistake early on can change everything that follows. So I think we need to train and evaluate the entire interaction, including whether the agent can recover when its initial approach fails.

One promising direction is to give agents a much broader distribution of problems and environments, with feedback that rewards actually completing the task. But we also have to be careful: an agent can become very good at the environments we train it in without learning something transferable. The real test is whether it can enter an unfamiliar situation, figure out what matters, and make progress with limited feedback.

So I would frame this as a combination of learning general capabilities during training and learning efficiently from experience during execution. We need both.

r001.rationale: The response warns that agents may fail to transfer beyond training environments, but it does not identify confinement to evaluation benchmarks as the risk.

r002.rationale: The response proposes broader training and learning from experience, but does not suggest using AI more to train AI.
